summary: This unit covers how neurons and muscle cells hold a resting voltage, fire action potentials, pass signals across synapses, and conduct them along axons. Exam questions ask you to predict what happens when potassium shifts, when myelin is lost, when the neuromuscular junction is blocked, and when firing becomes abnormally synchronized in a seizure.

points: The Na+/K+ ATPase pumps 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in per ATP, which keeps the gradients and adds a few millivolts of negativity.
At rest the membrane is most permeable to K+ through leak channels, so the resting potential sits close to the K+ equilibrium potential.
Nernst equation at body temperature: E = (61.5 / z) x log([ion outside] / [ion inside]) in mV. E for K+ is about -90 mV; E for Na+ is about +60 mV.
Resting potential is about -70 mV in neurons and about -90 mV in skeletal muscle.
Hyperkalemia shrinks the K+ gradient and depolarizes the cell; a mild rise makes cells easier to fire, but sustained depolarization inactivates Na+ channels and causes weakness and arrhythmias.
Hypokalemia hyperpolarizes the cell, moving it farther from threshold, which causes weakness or flaccid paralysis.
Threshold (about -55 mV in neurons) opens voltage-gated Na+ channels; Na+ rushes in and the upstroke heads toward E for Na+.
Within about 1 ms the Na+ channel inactivation gate closes, and slower voltage-gated K+ channels open, so K+ leaves and the cell repolarizes.
K+ channels close slowly, so the membrane briefly dips below the resting potential toward E for K+ (afterhyperpolarization).
Absolute refractory period: Na+ channels are inactivated, so no stimulus of any size can fire another spike.
Relative refractory period: some Na+ channels have recovered but K+ conductance is still high, so only a stronger than normal stimulus fires a spike.
The action potential is all or none and travels without losing size.
EPSPs are small depolarizations from ligand-gated cation channels (for example AMPA receptors letting Na+ in).
IPSPs hold the cell below threshold by letting Cl- in (GABA-A, glycine receptors) or K+ out (GABA-B).
Temporal summation: one synapse fires repeatedly, and each potential adds to the last before it fades.
Spatial summation: many synapses fire at the same time, and their potentials add together.
The axon hillock (initial segment) has the densest voltage-gated Na+ channels, so it has the lowest threshold and is where the net sum triggers the spike.
Myelin raises membrane resistance and lowers capacitance, so current spreads farther and faster along the internode.
Voltage-gated Na+ channels cluster at the nodes of Ranvier, so the spike regenerates only at nodes (saltatory conduction).
A wider axon has less internal resistance, so it conducts faster. Large myelinated A-alpha fibers are fastest; thin unmyelinated C fibers are slowest.
Oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS axons (one cell, many axons); Schwann cells myelinate PNS axons (one cell per internode).
Demyelination lets current leak out across the bare segment, so conduction slows; if too little current reaches the next node, conduction blocks.
Multiple sclerosis strips CNS myelin; Guillain-Barré syndrome strips peripheral nerve myelin. Heat worsens conduction in demyelinated axons (Uhthoff phenomenon).
The nerve action potential opens presynaptic voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (P/Q type), and Ca2+ enters the terminal.
SNARE proteins (synaptobrevin on the vesicle, syntaxin and SNAP-25 on the membrane) fuse vesicles and release acetylcholine.
Acetylcholine binds nicotinic receptors (ligand-gated cation channels) on the end plate, producing an end-plate potential that fires the muscle.
Acetylcholinesterase in the cleft splits acetylcholine into acetate and choline, ending the signal; choline is taken back up.
A seizure is excessive, synchronous firing of cortical neurons when excitation (glutamate) outweighs inhibition (GABA).
Focal seizures start in one hemisphere and occur with or without impaired awareness; they can spread to both sides (focal to bilateral tonic-clonic).
Generalized seizures involve both hemispheres from the start: tonic-clonic (stiffening, then jerking, then postictal confusion) or absence.
Absence seizures: a child has brief staring spells with no postictal confusion, often triggered by hyperventilation; EEG shows 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges.
Febrile seizures occur in children about 6 months to 5 years old with fever of 38 °C (100.4 °F) or higher and no CNS infection; simple ones are brief and generalized and carry a good outlook.
Hypokalemic periodic paralysis is an inherited (usually autosomal dominant) skeletal muscle Ca2+ or Na+ channel defect causing attacks of flaccid weakness with low serum K+.
Attacks follow carbohydrate-rich meals (insulin drives K+ into cells) or rest after exercise; potassium is normal between attacks.

tricks.label: Resting potential follows potassium
tricks.text: Whatever ion the membrane is most permeable to pulls the voltage toward its own equilibrium potential. At rest that is K+, so any change in serum K+ moves the resting potential.

tricks.label: Use it and lose it, or use it and gain it
tricks.text: Myasthenia gravis weakens with repeated effort as acetylcholine stores run down. Lambert-Eaton improves with repeated effort because Ca2+ builds up in the terminal.

tricks.label: Thick and wrapped is fast
tricks.text: Two things speed conduction: a wider axon (less internal resistance) and myelin (current jumps node to node). Remove either and velocity drops.

highYield: Resting potential sits near E for K+ because K+ leak channels dominate at rest.
Hyperkalemia depolarizes the resting membrane and, if sustained, inactivates Na+ channels and lowers excitability.
Absolute refractory period comes from Na+ channel inactivation; relative refractory period from lingering K+ efflux.
The axon hillock fires first because it has the highest density of voltage-gated Na+ channels.
Demyelination slows conduction or blocks it outright; heat makes demyelinated conduction worse.
Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins and blocks acetylcholine release.
Child with brief staring spells and 3 Hz spike-and-wave on EEG: absence seizures.
Young man with flaccid weakness after a carbohydrate-heavy meal and low K+: hypokalemic periodic paralysis.
pitfalls: A mild K+ rise makes cells easier to fire, but a sustained rise keeps Na+ channels inactivated and causes weakness.
Absence seizures have no postictal confusion; a staring spell followed by confusion suggests a focal seizure with impaired awareness.
Myasthenia gravis is a postsynaptic problem; Lambert-Eaton and botulism are presynaptic problems.
Hypokalemic periodic paralysis shows low K+ only during attacks; a normal K+ between attacks does not rule it out.

Peak approaches E for Na+ (about +60 mV) but does not reach it
Repolarization from Na+ channel inactivation plus voltage-gated K+ efflux
Afterhyperpolarization from K+ channels closing slowly, toward E for K+
Absolute refractory period while Na+ channels are inactivated
Relative refractory period needs a stronger stimulus

summary: The brain runs almost entirely on glucose and needs several vitamins and cofactors to make energy, neurotransmitters, and myelin. This unit links each nutrient or toxin to the enzyme it affects and to the neurologic picture you will see on the exam: Wernicke encephalopathy, subacute combined degeneration, pellagra, hepatic encephalopathy, the sphingolipidoses, and lead poisoning.

points: Glucose crosses the blood-brain barrier through GLUT1 on endothelial cells and enters neurons through GLUT3; neither needs insulin.
The brain stores almost no glycogen and fatty acids are not a meaningful brain fuel, so it needs a steady glucose supply.
After several days of fasting the liver makes ketone bodies (acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate), and the brain shifts to using them, sparing glucose and muscle protein.

Hypoglycemia first causes adrenergic symptoms (sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger), then neuroglycopenic symptoms (confusion, behavior change, blurred vision, seizures, coma) as glucose falls further.
Thiamine pyrophosphate is a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase, and transketolase.
Without it, glucose cannot be fully oxidized, so ATP falls in the brain and heart.
Wernicke encephalopathy: confusion, ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus, and ataxia; lesions in the mammillary bodies, medial thalamus, and periaqueductal gray.
Korsakoff syndrome adds lasting memory loss with confabulation.
Dry beriberi is a symmetric peripheral neuropathy with muscle wasting; wet beriberi is high-output heart failure.
Giving glucose before thiamine pushes more flux through thiamine-dependent enzymes, uses up the last thiamine, and can trigger or worsen Wernicke encephalopathy.
Methionine synthase (needs B12, uses methyl-THF from folate) converts homocysteine to methionine, so both deficiencies raise homocysteine.
Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (needs B12 only) converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA, so only B12 deficiency raises methylmalonic acid.
Both cause megaloblastic anemia from impaired DNA synthesis.

B12 deficiency damages myelin: subacute combined degeneration of the dorsal columns (lost vibration and position sense) and lateral corticospinal tracts (spastic weakness, Babinski sign), plus peripheral neuropathy and cognitive decline.
Folate deficiency spares the nervous system; giving folate alone can fix the anemia of B12 deficiency while nerve damage keeps progressing.
The brain has no complete urea cycle; astrocytes clear ammonia with glutamine synthetase (glutamate + NH3 to glutamine).
Glutamine builds up inside astrocytes and pulls in water, so astrocytes swell and cerebral edema follows.
Using up glutamate and alpha-ketoglutarate disturbs neurotransmission and slows the TCA cycle.
Alzheimer type II astrocytes (enlarged, pale nuclei in gray matter) are the hallmark of hyperammonemia, seen in liver failure and Wilson disease.
Causes: liver failure, portosystemic shunting, and urea cycle defects such as ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency. Signs: asterixis, confusion, somnolence, coma.
Myelin is about 70 to 80 percent lipid by dry weight, rich in cholesterol, galactocerebroside, sulfatide, and sphingomyelin.
Sphingolipids are broken down step by step in lysosomes; a missing enzyme lets its substrate build up in neurons or myelin.
Sphingolipidoses with neuronal storage (Tay-Sachs, Niemann-Pick type A) cause progressive loss of milestones in infancy.
Leukodystrophies destroy myelin: Krabbe disease and metachromatic leukodystrophy are lysosomal; X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy is a peroxisomal defect with very long chain fatty acid buildup.
Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase (ALA builds up) and ferrochelatase (protoporphyrin builds up, measured as zinc protoporphyrin).
Heme synthesis fails, giving a microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling of red cells.
Children (old paint chips and dust) get encephalopathy with cerebral edema, learning problems, and developmental delay.
Adults (batteries, smelting, ammunition) get a peripheral motor neuropathy with wrist drop and foot drop, plus abdominal colic and nephropathy.

tricks.label: Think ATP
tricks.text: Thiamine pyrophosphate enzymes: Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, Transketolase, Pyruvate dehydrogenase.

tricks.label: The 3 Ds of pellagra
tricks.text: Dermatitis, Diarrhea, Dementia (and death if untreated) from niacin deficiency.

tricks.label: LEAD
tricks.text: Lead lines on gums and bones, Encephalopathy and Erythrocyte basophilic stippling, Abdominal colic and sideroblastic Anemia, Drops (wrist and foot).

tricks.label: MMA decides B12 vs folate
tricks.text: Both raise homocysteine. Only B12 runs methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, so a high methylmalonic acid means B12 and means the nerves are at risk.

highYield: GLUT1 at the blood-brain barrier and GLUT3 on neurons are insulin independent.
In prolonged fasting the brain switches to ketone bodies.
Malnourished patient with confusion, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia: give thiamine before glucose.
High methylmalonic acid plus dorsal column and corticospinal signs: B12 deficiency (subacute combined degeneration).
Isoniazid causes B6 deficiency, which can cause seizures and neuropathy.
Hyperammonemia swells astrocytes through glutamine buildup; look for Alzheimer type II astrocytes.
Cherry-red macula with no hepatosplenomegaly: Tay-Sachs; with hepatosplenomegaly: Niemann-Pick.
Adult battery worker with wrist drop, colic, and basophilic stippling: lead poisoning.
pitfalls: Vitamin E deficiency mimics B12 deficiency (dorsal columns, ataxia) but has normal methylmalonic acid and no megaloblastic anemia.
Folate fixes the anemia of B12 deficiency but not the nerve damage, so check B12 before giving folate.
Alzheimer type II astrocytes are a sign of hyperammonemia and have nothing to do with Alzheimer disease.
Adrenoleukodystrophy is peroxisomal; Krabbe and metachromatic leukodystrophy are lysosomal.

summary: Neurotransmitters are built from amino acids and simple precursors by a few key enzymes, then broken down into products you can measure in urine. Exam questions ask you to trace each pathway, name the rate-limiting enzyme or cofactor, link breakdown products to tumors, and match each transmitter to its source nucleus and the diseases that change it.

points: Phenylalanine to tyrosine by phenylalanine hydroxylase (needs BH4).
Tyrosine to L-DOPA by tyrosine hydroxylase (needs BH4); this is the rate-limiting step.
L-DOPA to dopamine by aromatic L-amino acid (DOPA) decarboxylase, which needs pyridoxal phosphate (B6).
Dopamine to norepinephrine by dopamine beta-hydroxylase inside vesicles; it needs vitamin C (and copper).
Norepinephrine to epinephrine by PNMT, which uses SAM as the methyl donor; cortisol from the adrenal cortex induces PNMT in the adrenal medulla.
Most catecholamine action ends by reuptake into the nerve terminal; the rest is broken down by MAO (mitochondria) and COMT (cytosol, mostly liver).
Dopamine breaks down to homovanillic acid (HVA).
Norepinephrine breaks down to normetanephrine and vanillylmandelic acid (VMA); epinephrine to metanephrine and VMA.
Neuroblastoma raises urinary HVA and VMA; pheochromocytoma raises plasma and urine metanephrines.
Tryptophan to 5-hydroxytryptophan by tryptophan hydroxylase (needs BH4), the rate-limiting step.
5-hydroxytryptophan to serotonin by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (B6).
Brain serotonin comes from the raphe nuclei of the brainstem.
In the pineal gland serotonin is converted to melatonin; darkness increases melatonin release through a pathway from the suprachiasmatic nucleus.
MAO breaks serotonin down to 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA), which rises in urine in carcinoid syndrome.
Glutamate is the main excitatory transmitter: AMPA receptors pass Na+ for fast EPSPs; NMDA receptors pass Ca2+ once depolarization removes their Mg2+ block.
GABA is made from glutamate by glutamate decarboxylase, which needs pyridoxal phosphate (B6).
GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter in the brain (GABA-A is a Cl- channel; GABA-B is G protein coupled and opens K+ channels).
Glycine is the main inhibitory transmitter in the spinal cord and brainstem and opens Cl- channels.
Excitotoxicity in ischemia: ATP fails, neurons depolarize, and glutamate reuptake stops, so glutamate floods the synapse.
Excess NMDA activation lets Ca2+ pour in, which activates proteases, phospholipases, and free radical production and kills the neuron.
Choline acetyltransferase joins acetyl-CoA and choline to make acetylcholine in the nerve terminal.
Acetylcholinesterase in the synaptic cleft splits it into acetate and choline; choline is recycled into the terminal.
Cholinergic neurons of the nucleus basalis of Meynert project to the cortex and are lost early in Alzheimer disease, lowering cortical acetylcholine.

charts.title: Synthesis and breakdown at a glance

tricks.label: Walk the catecholamine ladder
tricks.text: Phenylalanine, tyrosine, DOPA, dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine. Each rung adds one change: a hydroxyl, a hydroxyl, remove CO2, a hydroxyl, then a methyl.

tricks.label: Name the breakdown by the parent
tricks.text: HVA comes from dopamine. VMA and metanephrines come from norepinephrine and epinephrine. 5-HIAA comes from serotonin.

tricks.label: B6 makes the signals
tricks.text: Pyridoxal phosphate runs the decarboxylases that make GABA, dopamine, and serotonin. Low B6 means low GABA, which is why deficiency causes seizures.

highYield: Tyrosine hydroxylase is rate limiting for catecholamines; tryptophan hydroxylase for serotonin.
Dopamine beta-hydroxylase needs vitamin C.
Cortisol induces PNMT, so the adrenal medulla makes mostly epinephrine.
Child with an abdominal mass and high urinary HVA and VMA: neuroblastoma.
High urinary 5-HIAA: carcinoid syndrome.
Glutamate excitotoxicity through NMDA receptors and Ca2+ influx kills neurons after ischemia.
Parkinson disease: low dopamine from substantia nigra loss. Huntington disease: low GABA and acetylcholine, high dopamine.
Alzheimer disease: loss of cholinergic neurons in the nucleus basalis of Meynert.
pitfalls: Tyrosine hydroxylase (catecholamines) and tryptophan hydroxylase (serotonin) are both BH4 dependent; do not mix up their substrates.
GABA is made from glutamate, so the brain's main inhibitory transmitter comes from its main excitatory one.
Glycine is the main inhibitory transmitter in the spinal cord; GABA dominates in the brain.
Neuroblastoma is screened with HVA and VMA; pheochromocytoma is screened with metanephrines.

dumps.p: Starting from phenylalanine, draw the pathway to epinephrine. Label each enzyme and cofactor, mark the rate-limiting step, then draw the breakdown arrows to HVA and VMA.

Tyrosine hydroxylase makes L-DOPA, rate limiting (BH4)
DOPA decarboxylase makes dopamine (B6)
Dopamine beta-hydroxylase makes norepinephrine (vitamin C)
PNMT makes epinephrine (SAM, induced by cortisol)
MAO and COMT break down catecholamines
Dopamine to HVA; norepinephrine and epinephrine to VMA and metanephrines
High urinary HVA and VMA in neuroblastoma

Ventral tegmental area (midbrain): dopamine to limbic and frontal areas
Locus coeruleus (pons): norepinephrine

Nucleus basalis of Meynert (basal forebrain): acetylcholine; lost in Alzheimer disease

summary: Many neurologic diseases come from a specific kind of genetic error: repeat expansions, extra chromosomes, lost tumor suppressor genes, or amplified oncogenes. Exam questions give you a family history or a set of features and ask for the gene, the inheritance pattern, or the molecular mechanism.

points: A run of three bases grows past a threshold and disrupts the gene or its product.
Anticipation: repeats grow from one generation to the next, so onset comes earlier and disease is more severe.
Huntington repeats expand mainly through the father; fragile X expands through the mother, and congenital myotonic dystrophy comes from the mother.
Fragile X full mutation (more than about 200 CGG repeats) hypermethylates FMR1 and silences it.
Friedreich ataxia is autosomal recessive, so anticipation is not a feature; the GAA expansion lowers frataxin, a mitochondrial iron protein.
About 95 percent: meiotic nondisjunction, usually in maternal meiosis I; risk rises with maternal age.
About 4 percent: Robertsonian translocation (often 14;21); can be inherited from a parent with a balanced translocation and is not tied to maternal age.
About 1 percent: mosaicism from mitotic nondisjunction after fertilization; features are often milder.
The APP gene sits on chromosome 21, so an extra copy makes more amyloid-beta; Alzheimer plaques are present by about age 40 and dementia often follows.
NF1, NF2, tuberous sclerosis, and von Hippel-Lindau are autosomal dominant tumor suppressor disorders: one bad copy is inherited, and a tumor forms when the second copy is lost.
Neurofibromin is a Ras GTPase-activating protein; losing it leaves Ras switched on.
Hamartin (TSC1) and tuberin (TSC2) form a complex that normally restrains mTOR; losing either lets mTOR drive cell growth.
VHL protein normally targets HIF for breakdown; losing it raises HIF, which drives VEGF and erythropoietin.
Sturge-Weber syndrome is sporadic: a somatic activating GNAQ mutation causes a port-wine stain in the CN V1 area, ipsilateral leptomeningeal angioma, seizures, and glaucoma.
Autosomal recessive loss (usually deletion) of SMN1 on chromosome 5q; SMN2 copy number changes severity.
Anterior horn motor neurons degenerate, giving pure lower motor neuron signs.
Severe infantile form (type 1, Werdnig-Hoffmann): floppy infant, tongue fasciculations, areflexia, and respiratory failure; sensation and intellect are normal.

notes.h: Driver genes in nervous system tumors
points: Retinoblastoma: both copies of RB1 (chromosome 13q14) are lost (two-hit); Rb normally holds cells in G1 by binding E2F.
Hereditary retinoblastoma (germline first hit) is often bilateral and early, with later risk of osteosarcoma; sporadic cases are usually unilateral.
Oligodendroglioma is defined by an IDH1 or IDH2 mutation plus 1p/19q codeletion, which predicts better response to treatment.
Neuroblastoma with MYCN (N-myc) amplification behaves aggressively and has a poor prognosis.
Oncogenes need only one activated copy (gain of function); tumor suppressors need both copies lost.

tricks.label: X-Girlfriend's First Aid Helped Ace My Test
tricks.text: Fragile X: CGG. Friedreich ataxia: GAA. Huntington disease: CAG. Myotonic dystrophy: CTG.

tricks.label: Huntington CAG: Caudate has less ACh and GABA
tricks.text: The CAG repeat in Huntington disease destroys striatal neurons that make acetylcholine and GABA.

tricks.label: Count the chromosome letters
tricks.text: NF1 has 17 letters in neurofibromatosis (count them); NF2 is on 22, the number with two 2s; VHL has 3 letters and sits on chromosome 3.

highYield: Anticipation is seen in Huntington disease, fragile X, and myotonic dystrophy, but not in autosomal recessive Friedreich ataxia.
Fragile X silences FMR1 by hypermethylation of an expanded CGG repeat.
Down syndrome by Robertsonian translocation can recur in a family regardless of maternal age.
Extra APP on chromosome 21 leads to early-onset Alzheimer disease in Down syndrome.
Bilateral vestibular schwannomas: NF2 (merlin, chromosome 22).
Tuberous sclerosis: loss of hamartin or tuberin releases mTOR.
Floppy infant with tongue fasciculations and absent reflexes: spinal muscular atrophy (SMN1).
MYCN amplification in neuroblastoma predicts aggressive disease.
pitfalls: Sturge-Weber is sporadic and caused by an activating mutation, unlike the inherited tumor suppressor syndromes.
NF1, NF2, tuberous sclerosis, and von Hippel-Lindau are autosomal dominant (many cases are new mutations), yet each tumor still needs a second hit at the cellular level.
Spinal muscular atrophy causes lower motor neuron signs only; infant botulism also causes a floppy baby but adds constipation, ptosis, and sluggish pupils.
Huntington disease anticipation comes mainly from the father; myotonic dystrophy congenital disease comes from the mother.

Myotonic dystrophy: CTG, DMPK, autosomal dominant, anticipation

Friedreich: ataxia plus hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

summary: The hypothalamus controls the pituitary in two ways: releasing hormones carried by portal blood to the anterior lobe, and nerve axons that end in the posterior lobe. Exam questions ask you to predict what happens when a tumor, head injury, or surgery damages the chiasm, stalk, or posterior pituitary, and how stress and thyroid hormone change nervous system function.

points: Hypothalamic neurons release hormones into capillaries in the median eminence, which lies outside the blood-brain barrier.
Hypophyseal portal veins carry these hormones down the stalk to a second capillary bed in the anterior pituitary.
Releasing hormones: TRH, CRH, GnRH (must be pulsatile), and GHRH. Inhibiting hormones: somatostatin (GH, TSH) and dopamine (prolactin).
Dopamine from the arcuate nucleus tonically inhibits prolactin through D2 receptors, so prolactin is the one hormone that rises when the stalk is cut.
ADH is made mainly in the supraoptic nucleus and oxytocin mainly in the paraventricular nucleus.
Both travel down axons of the hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract with carrier proteins (neurophysins) and are released into blood in the posterior lobe.
ADH acts on V2 receptors in the collecting duct to insert aquaporin-2 and reabsorb water; release rises with high plasma osmolality or low blood volume.
Central diabetes insipidus (head trauma, pituitary surgery, craniopharyngioma): too little ADH, so large volumes of dilute urine with high serum sodium; urine concentrates after desmopressin.
SIADH (head trauma, meningitis, subarachnoid hemorrhage, CNS tumors, small cell lung cancer): too much ADH, so euvolemic hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine.
Correcting chronic hyponatremia too fast can cause osmotic demyelination syndrome in the pons.
The optic chiasm sits just above the pituitary; crossing nasal retinal fibers carry the temporal visual fields.
Pressing on the middle of the chiasm causes bitemporal hemianopia; a pituitary adenoma pushing up from below affects the upper temporal fields first.
Pituitary adenoma is the most common sellar mass in adults; prolactinoma is the most common hormone-making type.

Craniopharyngioma arises from Rathke pouch remnants, is often calcified and cystic, and is the most common sellar tumor in children (a second peak occurs in middle age); it causes visual loss, growth failure, and diabetes insipidus.
Stalk effect: a nonfunctioning mass blocks dopamine flow, so prolactin rises mildly while other pituitary hormones fall.
Lateral spread into the cavernous sinus can affect CN III, IV, V1, V2, and VI.
Fast arm: the hypothalamus drives sympathetic outflow; preganglionic fibers go straight to adrenal medulla chromaffin cells, which release mostly epinephrine within seconds.
Slow arm (HPA axis): paraventricular nucleus releases CRH, the anterior pituitary releases ACTH, and the adrenal cortex releases cortisol over minutes to hours.
Cortisol raises blood glucose, supports vascular tone by keeping catecholamine responses working, suppresses inflammation, and feeds back to inhibit CRH and ACTH.
Cortisol flows from the cortex into the medulla and induces PNMT, linking the two arms.

notes.h: Thyroid hormone and the nervous system
points: Thyroid hormone is needed for neuron growth, synapse formation, and myelination, most critically from late fetal life through the first years.
Congenital hypothyroidism causes intellectual disability and short stature if untreated; newborn screening allows early treatment that prevents this.
Hypothyroidism slows the relaxation phase of deep tendon reflexes and causes cognitive slowing and depression.
Hyperthyroidism causes fine tremor, hyperreflexia, anxiety, and insomnia, partly from increased beta-adrenergic sensitivity.

tricks.label: Cut the stalk, prolactin goes up
tricks.text: Every anterior pituitary hormone needs a hypothalamic push except prolactin, which needs a dopamine brake. Remove the hypothalamus and only prolactin rises.

tricks.label: SON makes water stay
tricks.text: Supraoptic nucleus makes ADH, which keeps water in. Paraventricular nucleus makes oxytocin (and CRH).

tricks.label: Below pushes up, above pushes down
tricks.text: A pituitary adenoma presses the chiasm from below and hits upper temporal fields first. A craniopharyngioma often presses from above and can hit lower temporal fields first.

highYield: Dopamine is the main inhibitor of prolactin; stalk compression causes mild hyperprolactinemia.
Pituitary adenoma compressing the chiasm causes bitemporal hemianopia.
Child with a calcified suprasellar mass, visual loss, and growth failure: craniopharyngioma.
Polyuria with dilute urine and high sodium after head trauma or pituitary surgery: central diabetes insipidus.
Hyponatremia with concentrated urine after subarachnoid hemorrhage or meningitis: SIADH.
ADH comes mainly from the supraoptic nucleus; oxytocin mainly from the paraventricular nucleus.
Cortisol induces PNMT, so the adrenal medulla makes mostly epinephrine.
Delayed relaxation of the ankle reflex is a classic sign of hypothyroidism.
pitfalls: A mildly raised prolactin with a large pituitary mass usually means stalk compression, while a very high prolactin points to a prolactinoma.
ADH and oxytocin are made in the hypothalamus; the posterior pituitary only stores and releases them.
Central diabetes insipidus responds to desmopressin; nephrogenic diabetes insipidus does not.
SIADH patients look euvolemic with a high urine sodium, which separates them from dehydrated patients with low sodium.

Portal veins carry them down the stalk to the anterior pituitary
TRH, CRH, GnRH, GHRH stimulate; somatostatin and dopamine inhibit
Supraoptic and paraventricular axons run down the stalk to the posterior pituitary
ADH and oxytocin are released into blood from the posterior lobe
The optic chiasm sits above the sella
Compression of crossing nasal fibers causes bitemporal hemianopia
Stalk compression blocks dopamine and raises prolactin

summary: The nervous system is partly shielded from immune attack by the blood-brain barrier, yet many neurologic diseases are immune driven. This unit covers how meningitis inflames the brain, how autoimmunity strips myelin or blocks the neuromuscular junction, how tumors trigger paraneoplastic syndromes, and how vaccines against meningitis and polio build protection.

points: The barrier is built from endothelial tight junctions, a basement membrane, pericytes, and astrocyte foot processes.
It limits entry of immune cells, antibodies, complement, and many drugs, so normal CSF has very few cells and little complement.
Microglia are the resident macrophages of the CNS; they come from yolk sac (mesodermal) precursors, phagocytose debris, present antigen, and release cytokines.
In bacterial meningitis, microglia and macrophages sense bacterial products through toll-like receptors and release IL-1 and TNF-alpha.
These cytokines activate endothelium, recruit neutrophils, and open the barrier, causing vasogenic edema, raised intracranial pressure, and risk of herniation.
Typical CSF: many neutrophils, high protein, and low glucose.
Autoreactive CD4 T cells (Th1 making IFN-gamma, Th17 making IL-17) cross the barrier and attack CNS myelin; macrophages and microglia strip the myelin.
Strongest genetic link: HLA-DR2. It is most common in women aged 20 to 40.
CSF shows oligoclonal IgG bands (not present in serum) and a raised IgG index.
MRI shows white matter plaques around the lateral ventricles (periventricular).
Common findings: optic neuritis, internuclear ophthalmoplegia, sensory loss, weakness, symptoms that worsen with heat.
Weeks after Campylobacter jejuni diarrhea, antibodies made against bacterial lipooligosaccharide cross-react with peripheral nerve gangliosides (molecular mimicry).
Antibodies, complement, and macrophages damage peripheral myelin (or axons in the axonal variant).
Ascending symmetric weakness, areflexia, autonomic instability, and possible respiratory failure.
CSF shows high protein with a normal cell count (albuminocytologic dissociation).
Miller Fisher variant: anti-GQ1b antibodies (GQ1b is rich in the nerves that move the eyes) cause ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia.
Myasthenia gravis is type II hypersensitivity: antibodies to postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors block them, cause their internalization, and fix complement.
Myasthenia gravis is linked to thymic hyperplasia and thymoma.
Lambert-Eaton syndrome is type II hypersensitivity against presynaptic P/Q voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, often paraneoplastic with small cell lung cancer.
MS and acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM) are T cell-mediated (type IV); ADEM is a single episode of widespread demyelination, usually in a child, after a viral infection or vaccination.
A tumor expresses a protein also found in neurons; the immune response against the tumor attacks the nervous system too.
Neurologic symptoms often appear before the cancer is found.
Anti-Hu: small cell lung cancer, sensory neuronopathy, limbic encephalitis.
Anti-Yo (Purkinje cell antibody): ovarian or breast cancer, subacute cerebellar degeneration.
Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis: young woman with ovarian teratoma, psychiatric symptoms, seizures, abnormal movements, and autonomic instability.
Plain polysaccharide capsules trigger T cell-independent responses: mostly IgM, little memory, and poor responses in children under 2.
Conjugate vaccines (Hib, pneumococcal, meningococcal) link the polysaccharide to a protein carrier; B cells present carrier peptides to helper T cells.
T cell help brings class switching to IgG, affinity maturation, and memory, so the vaccine works in infants.
Inactivated polio vaccine (Salk) is injected and makes serum IgG that stops virus from reaching the CNS, with weak gut IgA.
Live oral polio vaccine (Sabin) makes both serum IgG and intestinal secretory IgA, blocking gut infection and spread; it rarely reverts and causes paralytic polio.

tricks.label: Hu is for the lung, Yo is for the ovary
tricks.text: Anti-Hu goes with small cell lung cancer and sensory loss. Anti-Yo goes with ovarian or breast cancer and cerebellar degeneration.

tricks.label: GQ1b moves the eyes
tricks.text: The GQ1b ganglioside is concentrated in the nerves to the eye muscles, so anti-GQ1b gives the eye findings of Miller Fisher syndrome.

tricks.label: Conjugate means T cell help
tricks.text: Sugar alone gets IgM and no memory. Add a protein carrier and helper T cells join in, giving IgG, memory, and protection in infants.

highYield: IL-1 and TNF-alpha open the blood-brain barrier in bacterial meningitis and cause cerebral edema.
Microglia are the resident macrophages of the CNS.
Multiple sclerosis: Th1 and Th17 T cells, HLA-DR2, oligoclonal IgG bands, periventricular plaques.
Guillain-Barré after Campylobacter jejuni: molecular mimicry with nerve gangliosides; high CSF protein with normal cells.
Anti-GQ1b: Miller Fisher variant with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia.
Myasthenia gravis and Lambert-Eaton are type II hypersensitivity; MS and ADEM are T cell-mediated.
Young woman with psychosis, seizures, and an ovarian teratoma: anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.
Conjugate vaccines turn a T cell-independent polysaccharide response into a T cell-dependent one.
pitfalls: Oligoclonal bands must be in the CSF and absent from serum to point to MS.
Guillain-Barré has a high CSF protein with a normal cell count; many white cells suggest infection instead.
Myasthenia gravis weakness worsens with use; Lambert-Eaton weakness improves with use.
The Sabin vaccine gives gut IgA and stops spread, but it can rarely revert, so only the Salk vaccine is safe for immunocompromised people.
